patches.old: When you open CARS, spend the first 30–45 seconds of each new passage doing a rapid triage assessment before committing to a full read.
patches.new: When you open CARS, spend about 20 seconds per passage — roughly 3 minutes across all nine — doing a rapid triage assessment before committing to a full read of any of them.
patches.reason: At 30–45 seconds each, previewing nine passages would take 4.5–7 minutes, contradicting the lesson's own 2–3 minute triage sprint.

patches.old: After 30 seconds, you should be able to place the passage in one of your three categories.
patches.new: After about 20 seconds, you should be able to place the passage in one of your three categories.
patches.reason: Keeps the protocol consistent with the 2–3 minute triage sprint.

patches.old: - Spend the first 2–3 minutes of the section previewing all 9 passages and marking them mentally (or using the flagging/scratch paper system) as green, yellow, or red.
patches.new: - Spend the first 2–3 minutes of the section previewing all 9 passages and marking them green, yellow, or red — mentally, with the exam's flag tool (Alt+F), or on the noteboard booklet the test center provides.
patches.reason: The MCAT supplies a noteboard booklet, not scratch paper; names the actual flag shortcut.

patches.old:
- Rapidly preview all 9 passages using the 30-second triage protocol
- Mentally (or on scratch paper) label each passage green, yellow, or red
patches.new:
- Rapidly preview all 9 passages using the ~20-second triage protocol
- Label each passage green, yellow, or red (mentally or on the noteboard booklet)
patches.reason: Consistency with the corrected triage timing, and the MCAT provides a noteboard booklet rather than scratch paper.

patches.old: The MCAT interface allows you to navigate freely between passages, which means you are not required to work sequentially from passage 1 to passage 9.
patches.new: The MCAT interface lets you move freely within a section — Alt+N and Alt+P step between questions, Alt+V opens a Navigator listing every question, and Alt+F flags one for review — so you are not required to work sequentially from passage 1 to passage 9.
patches.reason: Names the actual navigation tools so the strategy is executable on the real interface.

patches.old: The AAMC has consistently reported that CARS scores are among the strongest predictors of performance in medical school, particularly in clinical reasoning and communication.
patches.new: The AAMC's validity research reports that MCAT **total** scores correlate with preclerkship performance, clerkship performance, and USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 CK scores. (Those published findings are about total scores; claims singling out CARS as the best predictor of clinical reasoning or communication go beyond what the AAMC data show.)
patches.reason: AAMC validity findings are reported for total scores; the specific CARS claim is not supported, and MCAT scores correlate only weakly with direct-observation measures such as interpersonal skills.

patches.old: What is the primary risk of this time distribution?
patches.new: She therefore has 78 minutes left for the remaining 8 passages. What is the primary risk of this time distribution?
patches.reason: Supplies the arithmetic the stem needs; the figures given did not add up.

patches.old: finishing with 48 minutes for the remaining 7 passages.
patches.new: finishing that passage with 8 of the 9 passages still to go.
patches.reason: 12 minutes used leaves 78 minutes and 8 passages, not 48 minutes and 7 passages.

patches.old: Each CARS passage averages roughly 8-9 minutes in an optimal pacing plan.
patches.new: Each CARS passage averages roughly 10 minutes (90 minutes across 9 passage sets).
patches.reason: 90 minutes over 9 passages is about 10 minutes each, matching the lesson's own opening figure.

visual.title: A 90-minute plan
visual.alt: A 90-minute bar split into a 0 to 3 minute triage sprint, minutes 3 to 60 for green then yellow passages, minutes 60 to 85 for red passages, and minutes 85 to 90 to fill blanks, with checkpoints at 30 minutes (about 3 passages, 17 to 20 questions) and 60 minutes (about 6 passages, 35 to 38 questions). Three triage buckets: green, immediately accessible, done first while you are sharpest; yellow, manageable but denser, done second; red, your personal nightmare, done last so any shortfall falls where you would score least anyway. Four elimination filters for a stuck question: unsupported by the text, too extreme, out of scope, true but irrelevant. A box says that past 90 seconds on one question you should eliminate, guess, flag and move on, and a footer notes that triage is personal, a 7-question set is worth more than a 5-question set, and no answer should be left blank.
visual.caption: Timings are targets to practice against, not rules to obey on the day.
